title: Not the perfect body (section 20)
hookLine: the Tathagata isn't seen through a perfect body

lines: A PHOTO, A FACE, A MATCH.
cards: At a passport desk, an officer looks at a photo, then at the face in front of him, then back at the photo. The hair is different now; the face is older.
In a few seconds he decides the body matches and the person may pass. That's one kind of seeing, and it works well at a border. Section twenty of the Diamond Sutra asks whether it works for a Buddha.
If you had stood before the Buddha himself, perfect in form, would that body be where he is seen?

teach.b: First, the question. Can the Tathagata be seen through the perfect form of his body? The Sanskrit word for that body is rupakaya, the form-body, the Buddha you could have walked up to and looked at.
No, Subhuti says, because what the Tathagata calls the perfect form-body is not a perfect form-body; that is why it's called the perfect form-body.
Then the same question about the marks of a great being, and the same answer: the marks are no marks, and so they're called marks. We've met the marks before; today the weight is on the body itself.
Third, what isn't being said. The sutra doesn't say the Buddha had no body, or that his body didn't matter, or that the statues are wrong.
In Buddhist homes and temples, images of the Buddha are bowed to, offered flowers, kept with care. The sutra says something narrower and harder: the body isn't where the Tathagata is finally seen.
It's a doorway, not the room. Fourth, the mirror. Where are we seen?

teach.h: NO ONE IS ONLY THEIR BODY.
teach.b: Usually through a body first: its age, its size, its color, its clothes, how well it's working today.
A friend in a hospital bed is not their hospital bed. A grandparent who can't remember your name is not the forgetting. Section twenty doesn't make bodies unimportant.
It makes them not the last word.

how: Buddhists bow to and make offerings before images of the Buddha; Mahayana teachers use section 20 to say the Buddha is not finally found in a physical form, however perfect.

games.q: what does “not the perfect body” mean?
o: the sutra says the Buddha never had a body at all
statues of the Buddha are wrong and must be removed
the Buddha isn't finally seen through his body's perfect form

games.q: not the body: tap the pairs.
p: the marks of a great being

s: section 20 says the Buddha had no body
it says he is not seen through the perfect form-body, not that there was none.
the sutra asks the same question about the body and about the marks
both times the answer is no: x is not x, so it is called x.
section 20 says images of the Buddha should not be honored
it says nothing against images; it says where the Tathagata is finally seen.

games.q: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks: can the Tathagata be seen through the perfect form of his body? what do you say?
o: yes, the perfect body shows him
no, the perfect body is not a perfect body
games.why: Subhuti says no, and gives the same answer for the marks: they are no marks, and so they are called marks.

practice: Feel the body sitting, its weight, an ache somewhere, the face you'd see in a mirror, and notice the verdicts riding along: too tired, too old, not strong enough, fine today.

On each out-breath let a verdict soften, and ask quietly who is breathing here, apart from how this body looks or works today. You don't need an answer; let the body be a doorway for a few breaths, not the whole room.

wordCard.voice: Not the perfect body. Section twenty says the Tathagata is not seen through the perfect form-body, nor through the marks. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: form-body, the Buddha's visible body; section 20 says he is not seen through it.

carryVoice: Your line: not the body. A person is met somewhere a camera can't reach. See you tomorrow.
